title: CPR (Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation)
steps: Check the scene for safety before approaching.
Tap the person's shoulder and shout 'Are you OK?' to check responsiveness.
Call emergency services (or ask someone nearby to call).
Place the person on their back on a firm, flat surface.
Place the heel of one hand on the center of the chest (lower half of breastbone).
Place your other hand on top and interlock fingers.
Push hard and fast — at least 2 inches deep, at 100-120 compressions per minute.
Allow full chest recoil between compressions.
After 30 compressions, tilt the head back, lift the chin, and give 2 rescue breaths.
Continue 30:2 cycles until help arrives or the person starts breathing.
warnings: Do NOT stop CPR unless the person starts breathing or professional help takes over.
If you are untrained, do compression-only CPR (skip rescue breaths).
For infants, use two fingers instead of the heel of your hand.

title: Severe Bleeding Control
steps: Put on gloves or use a barrier (plastic bag) if available.
Apply direct pressure with a clean cloth or bandage to the wound.
Press firmly and do NOT remove the cloth — add more layers if blood soaks through.
If bleeding is from a limb, elevate it above heart level if possible.
For life-threatening limb bleeding, apply a tourniquet 2-3 inches above the wound.
Tighten the tourniquet until bleeding stops. Note the time of application.
Keep the person warm and lying down to prevent shock.
Monitor for signs of shock: pale skin, rapid breathing, confusion.
warnings: Do NOT remove embedded objects — stabilize them in place.
A tourniquet should only be loosened by medical professionals.
Apply pressure for at least 10 minutes before checking if bleeding has stopped.

title: Burn Treatment
steps: Remove the person from the heat source immediately.
Cool the burn with cool (not cold/ice) running water for at least 20 minutes.
Remove clothing and jewelry near the burn UNLESS stuck to the skin.
Cover the burn loosely with a sterile non-stick bandage or clean cloth.
For large burns, wrap the person in a clean sheet and keep them warm.
Give small sips of water if the person is conscious and able to swallow.
Elevate the burned area above heart level if possible.
warnings: Do NOT apply ice, butter, toothpaste, or any home remedies to burns.
Do NOT pop blisters — they protect against infection.
Chemical burns: brush off dry chemicals, then flush with water for 20+ minutes.
Seek emergency care for burns larger than the person's palm, or on face/hands/genitals.

title: Choking Response
steps: Ask 'Are you choking?' — if the person cannot speak, cough, or breathe, act immediately.
Stand behind the person and wrap your arms around their waist.
Make a fist with one hand and place it just above the navel, below the ribcage.
Grasp your fist with your other hand.
Perform quick, upward abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver).
Repeat thrusts until the object is expelled or the person becomes unconscious.
If the person becomes unconscious, lower them to the ground and begin CPR.
Check the mouth for the object before giving rescue breaths during CPR.
warnings: For pregnant women or obese individuals, perform chest thrusts instead.
For infants: alternate 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts.
Do NOT perform blind finger sweeps — only remove objects you can see.

title: Earthquake Response
steps: DROP to your hands and knees immediately.
Take COVER under a sturdy desk or table. Protect your head and neck.
HOLD ON to your shelter until shaking stops.
If no shelter is available, crouch near an interior wall away from windows.
If outdoors, move to an open area away from buildings, power lines, and trees.
If driving, pull over away from overpasses and bridges. Stay in the car.
After shaking stops, check yourself and others for injuries.
Be prepared for aftershocks — they can be as strong as the initial quake.
Check for gas leaks, damaged wiring, and structural damage before re-entering buildings.
Use text messages instead of calls to keep phone lines open for emergencies.
warnings: Do NOT run outside during shaking — falling debris is the #1 cause of injury.
Do NOT stand in doorways — this is a myth.
If near the coast after a major quake, move to high ground immediately (tsunami risk).

title: Flood Safety
steps: Move to higher ground immediately if flooding is imminent.
Do NOT walk, swim, or drive through flood waters.
Just 6 inches of moving water can knock you down; 1 foot can sweep a vehicle.
If trapped in a vehicle, get out immediately and move to higher ground.
If trapped in a building, move to the highest floor — do NOT go into the attic unless you can access the roof.
Signal for rescue from the roof or highest point if stranded.
Avoid contact with flood water — it may be contaminated with sewage or chemicals.
After flooding, do not return home until authorities say it is safe.
Document damage with photos for insurance before cleanup.
warnings: Turn Around, Don't Drown — never attempt to cross flooded roads.
Flood water can hide downed power lines, sharp debris, and sinkholes.
Boil tap water or use bottled water after flooding until water supply is confirmed safe.

title: Fire Emergency
steps: Alert everyone in the building — shout 'FIRE!' and activate the fire alarm.
Feel doors before opening — if hot, use an alternate exit.
Stay LOW to the ground where air is cleaner (crawl under smoke).
Cover your mouth and nose with a wet cloth if possible.
Exit the building using stairs — NEVER use elevators during a fire.
If clothes catch fire: STOP, DROP to the ground, and ROLL to smother flames.
Once outside, move at least 150 feet from the building.
Call emergency services from a safe location.
Do NOT re-enter a burning building for any reason.
Account for all occupants at a designated meeting point.
warnings: Smoke inhalation kills more people than flames — stay low.
If trapped, seal door gaps with wet towels and signal from a window.
Never open windows unless you need to signal for rescue — oxygen feeds fire.

title: Fracture & Bone Injury
steps: Keep the injured area still — do NOT attempt to straighten a broken bone.
Apply a splint above and below the fracture to immobilize the area.
Use any rigid material (sticks, boards, rolled magazines) as a splint.
Pad the splint with soft material (cloth, towels) for comfort.
Secure the splint with tape, belts, or torn fabric strips.
Apply ice wrapped in cloth to reduce swelling (20 minutes on, 20 minutes off).
Elevate the injured limb above heart level if possible.
Monitor circulation below the injury — check for numbness, tingling, or color change.
For suspected spinal injury, do NOT move the person — stabilize the head and neck.
warnings: Do NOT move someone with a suspected spine or neck injury.
If bone is protruding through skin (open fracture), cover with clean dressing — do NOT push it back.
Check pulse below the fracture — loss of pulse is a medical emergency.

title: Treating Shock
steps: Call emergency services immediately — shock is life-threatening.
Have the person lie down on their back.
Elevate the legs about 12 inches (unless you suspect head, neck, or back injury).
Keep the person warm with blankets or coats.
Do NOT give the person anything to eat or drink.
Loosen tight clothing, belts, or restrictive gear.
If the person vomits, turn them on their side to prevent choking.
Monitor breathing and pulse continuously.
If breathing stops, begin CPR immediately.
Keep the person calm and reassured until help arrives.
warnings: Signs of shock: pale/gray skin, rapid weak pulse, rapid breathing, confusion, nausea.
Anaphylactic shock: use an epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen) if available.
Do NOT elevate legs if there is a head, neck, back, or leg injury.

title: Poisoning Response
steps: Call Poison Control or emergency services immediately.
Try to identify the poison: what substance, how much, when ingested.
If the person is conscious, do NOT induce vomiting unless told to by Poison Control.
If poison is on the skin, remove contaminated clothing and rinse skin with water for 20 minutes.
If poison is in the eyes, flush with clean water for 15-20 minutes.
If inhaled poison, move the person to fresh air immediately.
Save any containers, labels, or samples of the substance for emergency responders.
If the person is unconscious, place them in the recovery position (on their side).
Monitor breathing — begin CPR if breathing stops.
warnings: Do NOT give activated charcoal unless directed by medical professionals.
Do NOT induce vomiting for corrosive substances (acids, bleach) or petroleum products.
Carbon monoxide poisoning is odorless — evacuate immediately if CO detector alarms.
